title: A Shoot from the Stump of Jesse
summary: Out of the cut-down stump of David's family line a new king will grow, filled with the Spirit of the LORD, who judges the poor with justice and strikes down the wicked by his word. His reign brings a peace so deep that predators and prey lie down together and the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD. On that day God will gather his scattered people from every direction, heal the old split between Ephraim and Judah, and make a highway home as he once did out of Egypt.
story: Chapter 10 ended with the LORD felling the proud forest of Assyria like a woodsman with an axe. Chapter 11 turns at once to another stump, the house of Jesse, David's father. The royal line of David, which God had promised to keep on the throne (2 Samuel 7), looked in Isaiah's day like a tree cut to the ground: kings such as Ahaz had trusted Assyria instead of God, and the prophet had warned that judgment would leave only a remnant. Yet from that stump a shoot will grow. This chapter gathers up the royal promises of chapters 7 and 9 (the child Immanuel, the son whose government has no end) and describes the king himself and the world his reign makes. Chapter 12 answers with the song the rescued people will sing.
historical:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 BC, the year King Uzziah died, into the reign of Hezekiah around 700 BC. These were the decades when the Assyrian Empire, based in northern Mesopotamia, swept west. Under Tiglath-pileser III (reigned about 745 to 727 BC) and his successors, Assyria turned small kingdoms into vassals or provinces. The northern kingdom of Israel, often called Ephraim after its leading tribe, fell when Samaria was taken in 722 BC and much of its population was deported. Judah survived as a tribute-paying vassal, and in 701 BC Sennacherib ravaged its cities and besieged Jerusalem.

The list of lands in verse 11 reflects that world of deportation and flight. Assyria and Egypt were the two great powers; Pathros is Upper (southern) Egypt; Cush is the Nile kingdom south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan; Elam lay east of Babylonia in what is now southwestern Iran; Shinar is the old name for Babylonia; Hamath was a city-state on the Orontes River in Syria; and the islands or coastlands of the sea are the Mediterranean shores to the west. Many scholars date parts of verses 10 to 16 later than Isaiah, pointing to the widespread scattering it assumes, while others note that Israelites were already being deported and fleeing in all these directions during the Assyrian age.
cultural:
Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to champion the widow, the orphan, and the poor; royal inscriptions and law codes boast of it, and Psalm 72 prays for it. Isaiah's point is that the kings he knew had failed at exactly this (see 10:1-2). The new king will not decide cases by appearances or hearsay, the ordinary weaknesses of a royal court, but with righteousness. His weapon is his word: a rod of the mouth and the breath of the lips. The belt and sash of verse 5 are the garments a man tied around his waist to get ready for action, so righteousness and faithfulness are what he is dressed in for work.

The animals of verses 6 to 8 were no abstraction to Isaiah's hearers. Wolves, leopards, bears, and lions still lived in the land, and a shepherd guarding goats and lambs knew them as real threats. Cobras and vipers were a daily danger to children in fields and houses. The picture of a small child leading them all, and a toddler putting a hand into a snake's den, speaks to the fears of an agricultural village. The banner of verses 10 and 12 was a signal pole raised on a hill to rally troops or call people to gather.
literary: The chapter has two panels. Verses 1 to 9 are poetry describing the king (verses 1 to 5) and the peace of his realm (verses 6 to 9). The imagery runs from plant to person to world: shoot, branch, and root; the Spirit resting on him in three pairs (wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and fear of the LORD); then a series of predators paired with their natural prey. Verse 9 is the hinge, closing with the famous line that “the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.” Verses 10 to 16, marked twice by “On that day”, widen the lens to the nations and the exiles. They are built on an exodus pattern: God raises his hand a second time, dries up the sea, splits the river, and builds a highway, “as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.”

outline.t: The king from Jesse's stump, filled with the Spirit and judging with justice
The peace of his realm: predators and prey together on the holy mountain
The Root of Jesse as a banner for the nations and the gathering of the exiles
Ephraim and Judah reconciled and a new exodus highway home

doctrines.note: The chapter describes a king from David's line whose rule is marked by the Spirit, justice for the poor, and a word that judges the wicked. This became one of the central texts for Jewish and Christian hope in an anointed king, a messiah.

The Spirit of the LORD rests on the king and equips him with wisdom, counsel, strength, and the fear of the LORD. In the Old Testament the Spirit empowers leaders for their task; here that empowering is permanent and complete.

God's reign through his king reaches beyond Israel's politics to the whole created order, so that nothing harms or destroys on his holy mountain. Justice for the lowly and peace in creation belong together.
Hope grows from a stump. The chapter refuses to deny that judgment has cut the tree down, yet it insists that God's promise outlives the failure of the people who carried it.

words.note: Choter, a shoot or twig, the thin new growth that springs from a stump. The word is humble on purpose: after the mighty cedars of Assyria are felled in chapter 10, God's king begins as a sprout. It paints the Messiah's origin as small and unlikely rather than grand.

Netser, a branch or green sprout from the roots, parallel to the shoot in verse 1. Some early Christian readers linked this word with Nazareth and with Matthew's comment that Jesus would be called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23), though Matthew does not cite a single verse and the connection is debated.

Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. It appears four times in verse 2 alone as the Spirit of the LORD resting on the king, and again in verse 4 where he slays the wicked with the breath of his lips. The same word ties his inner equipping to the power of his speech.

Nes, a banner or signal pole. In verses 10 and 12 the Root of Jesse himself becomes the rallying point to which the nations turn and around which the exiles gather. Isaiah uses the image elsewhere for God summoning armies (5:26); here it summons peoples to peace.

christ: The New Testament hears Jesus in this chapter directly. Paul quotes verse 10 in its Greek form, the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament), to show that the nations would hope in the root of Jesse (Romans 15:12). The Spirit resting on the king echoes the Spirit descending on Jesus at his baptism (Mark 1:10), and Paul pictures the returning Lord slaying the lawless one with the breath of his mouth (2 Thessalonians 2:8). Revelation shows the one who judges with a sword from his mouth (Revelation 19:15). The chapter's scope also explains why Christians read it in two stages: the king has come and the nations are seeking him, but the world where the lion eats straw and nothing harms or destroys still waits for his return.

hard.q: Will wolves and lions literally stop eating meat, or is this poetry?
hard.a: Readers take verses 6 to 9 in different ways. Some read them literally, as a description of a renewed creation (either in a future earthly reign of Christ or in the new heavens and new earth) where violence among animals truly ends, noting that Genesis 1 gives plants as food and that Romans 8 speaks of creation's release from bondage. Others read the animals as a picture of peoples and nations, with the fierce powers living at peace with the weak, a reading supported by the way Isaiah uses animal imagery for nations elsewhere. Many hold both: the passage is poetry, but the poetry is about a real renewal of the whole world, not only of human hearts. What the text plainly teaches on every reading is that the Messiah's reign ends harm and destruction and fills the earth with the knowledge of God.

questions: The king in verses 3 and 4 does not judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear. How do appearances and hearsay shape your own judgments of people?
Why do you think Isaiah pictures God's hope beginning from a stump rather than a healthy tree? Where have you seen something new grow from what looked finished?
Verse 13 imagines old rivals, Ephraim and Judah, no longer envying or harassing each other. What long-standing rivalry among God's people would you most like to see healed?
